title: Tool‑Augmented Post‑Processing of Identical LLM Candidates for Intent‑Driven Network Configuration (shared_initial_candidate evaluation)
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1) that isolates the effect of deterministic post‑processing (a NetOps verifier + lightweight topology simulator) on deterministic validator pass/fail outcomes when the same single LLM candidate is reused across conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Planned: 300 paired tasks (600 episodes); completed: 598 episodes → 299 complete pairs. For the 299 analyzable pairs the archived contingency is n11=299, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0; both baseline and guarded arms accepted the identical candidates (299/299). Paired difference = 0.00; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10k resamples, seed=1729). All raw outputs, provider traces, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, and execution logs are archived with SHA‑256 hashes (see Disclosure). Because the design fixes generation (shared candidate), these results answer only whether downstream verifier/simulator post‑processing changes deterministic validator outcomes for identical candidates; they do not address whether independent agentic, tool‑augmented generation would produce different or safer candidates. We report full execution accounting, a missingness post‑mortem, and practical recommendations for follow‑up independent‑generation evaluations.

sections.introduction: Intent‑driven network configuration (intent→config) aims to translate high‑level operator objectives into low‑level device commands. Recent approaches pair generative LLMs with deterministic validators, simulators and repair loops to increase operational safety. However, empirical claims that such tool chains improve operational correctness can conflate generator improvements with verifier or repair effects. We designed a narrowly scoped, fully preregistered paired experiment to isolate downstream tooling effects by fixing generation: for each task a single LLM candidate (the shared_initial_candidate) was produced and reused verbatim by both the baseline and the guarded pipelines. Research question (preregistered): does applying a deterministic verifier and simulator as post‑processing change the deterministic‑validator pass/fail outcome for identical LLM candidates? The experiment, execution artifacts, and analysis are archived and hashed; we report the artifact‑grounded outcome and its limitations.
sections.related_work: Related work spans intent→configuration translation with LLMs (intent‑to‑config systems and pretrained configuration models), tool‑augmented agent designs, and generate–validate–repair pipelines. Representative verified leads: intent‑based configuration and LLM translation (Nguyen et al., 2024; doi:10.1002/nem.2313), PreConfig (arXiv:2403.09369), agentic tool architectures and domain tool design (preprints and RAG studies, e.g., 10.20944/preprints202604.1820.v1), and reliability/validator studies (e.g., WeClaw-like runtime work and verifier‑tax tradeoffs, 10.2139/ssrn.7317098, 10.5220/0013221900003890). Those works motivated isolating tooling effects; our contribution is a preregistered, artifact‑anchored run that holds generation constant to measure only post‑generation tooling impact.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand. The preregistration cand_netops_toolagent_003_v1 was frozen prior to execution (SHA‑256: 991674d51794b41cf66471509149237b9a99f709b69aa3408d3d9d2ea2d50fc0). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline on a deterministic‑validator pass indicator, tested with exact McNemar (two‑sided) and a bootstrap (percentile) 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Key fixed semantics: shared_initial_candidate — per preregistration, one LLM generation was produced per task and reused verbatim by both pipelines; this is central to the estimand and to the interpretation of results. Experimental design and implementation. Adapter/orchestration: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Declared model: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json; artifact SHA‑256: 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Deterministic verifier used: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Task bank: deterministic synthetic topology templates with explicit initial and expected final states and per‑task difficulty metadata; confirmatory sample = 300 paired tasks (planned). Generation and call budget: one shared initial generation per task, maximum model calls per preregistration = 600 (one shared generation + repair allowance), final model_calls_used = 300 (execution manifest). Inclusion/exclusion and missingness: exact matches to a curated public config corpus were predesignated for exploratory exclusion; technical failures are logged and treated per the preregistered missingness plan (complete‑pair primary analysis, sensitivity treating failed runs as verifier‑fail). Logging and provenance. All provider calls, raw model outputs, validator traces, scoring JSONs, task manifests, and execution logs were archived and SHA‑256 hashed; authoritative manifests and hashes are provided in the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json; many per‑file SHA‑256s are available under execution/*).
sections.results: Execution accounting (artifact‑backed). Planned episodes: 600 (300 pairs). Completed episodes: 598. Failed episodes: 2 (together forming one missing pair, pair‑000269). Complete pairs available for analysis: 299. Model calls used: 300 (completed host model calls: 299; failed host model call events: 1; these counts are recorded in execution/provider_calls/* and summarized in the execution manifest). Confirmatory outcome (archival counts). For the 299 analyzable pairs the verified contingency table is: n11 = 299, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (artifact: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 d77df43abf83e081bb5a3c3a21fa0de67afd72628ee5ed880f2bff810e627174). Baseline successes = 299/299 (100.0%); guarded successes = 299/299 (100.0%). Paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Bootstrap (10,000 resamples, seed=1729) percentile 95% CI for the paired difference = [0.00, 0.00]. Representative scored episodes and validator traces. We include three representative scored episodes and their archived scoring JSONs and response texts: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (sha256: 6569b491...), execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (sha256: cefa6344...), and execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (sha256: 8f38c8be...). Each scoring record contains: normalized_response, raw_response_sha256, validator_trace with final_state snapshot, parsed/required command counts, difficulty metadata (e.g., pattern = shutdown_configure_restore), and the validator verdict. Missingness and failure post‑mortem. The sole missing pair (pair‑000269) arises from a failed shared_initial provider call; the failed provider event and the timestamp are recorded in the execution log (authoritative path: execution/execution_log.jsonl; SHA‑256: b45a600859502b088a9416744ccbff3f5fba2e6dd76b863440bdfd36ebf21bb8) and in the corresponding provider trace file execution/provider_calls/task-000269-shared-initial.json (recorded under execution/provider_calls/; see execution manifest). Per the preregistered missingness plan this pair was excluded from the primary complete‑pair analysis and the failure recorded as documented evidence (no re‑generation or manual substitution was performed).
sections.discussion: Interpretation and scope. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics — i.e., when the same single LLM candidate is reused verbatim by both pipelines — applying a deterministic verifier and simulator as post‑processing did not change deterministic validator pass/fail outcomes in our confirmatory set: both arms accepted the identical candidates in all 299 analyzable pairs. This is a narrowly scoped empirical fact rooted in archived artifacts and must not be interpreted as evidence about independent agentic generation or tool‑augmented candidate creation. Ceiling effect and power considerations. The preregistration assumed a baseline pass ≈ 0.60 and targeted detecting a +0.20 absolute paired improvement with n=300. Observed baseline pass = 1.00 (299/299), creating a ceiling effect that makes the preregistered minimally important effect unobservable in this execution. Reporting exact counts, an exact McNemar p‑value, and the degenerate bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00] is therefore the appropriate artifact‑grounded presentation; it avoids a misleading powered 'null' claim. Practical lessons for follow‑ups. To evaluate whether tool‑augmented agents (independent generation) materially improve operational safety compared with LLM‑only baselines, future preregistered experiments should: (1) adopt independent per‑condition generation semantics (not shared candidate reuse), (2) use a task bank stratified with genuinely adversarial or higher‑difficulty scenarios to avoid ceiling rates, (3) consider multiple model families and seeds, and (4) record identical comprehensive artifact logging and hashing as done here. Reproducibility and auditability. Deterministic validator traces supply explicit parsing, per‑command counts, final_state snapshots and violation codes that are useful for post‑deployment audits; these artifacts are archived per episode (execution/scoring/*, execution/responses/*, execution/provider_calls/*) together with full SHA‑256 manifests (execution_manifest). Operational implication: in settings where generator candidates are already high‑quality, the immediate marginal gain of verifier post‑processing to change the pass/fail outcome for the same candidate may be zero; however, validators remain indispensable for auditability, explicit violation signaling, and for driving repair heuristics in independent‑generation workflows.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a fully preregistered artifact‑anchored paired evaluation that isolates the effect of deterministic post‑processing on identical LLM candidates (shared_initial_candidate). For 299 analyzable pairs the archived, reproducible outcome is exact: both baseline and guarded pipelines accepted the same candidates (n11=299; no discordant pairs). The run and all reported numbers are anchored to execution and scoring artifacts (paths and SHA‑256 hashes are recorded in the execution manifest). Because the design fixed generation, these results do not answer whether independent agentic, tool‑augmented generation would produce different or safer outputs; that remains a separate estimand requiring a different preregistration and experimental design. We provide the execution accounting, the missingness post‑mortem (pair‑000269 recorded in execution/execution_log.jsonl; SHA‑256 b45a600859502b088a9416744ccbff3f5fba2e6dd76b863440bdfd36ebf21bb8), and a practical checklist for rigorous follow‑ups (independent generation, adversarial tasks, multi‑model replication).

limitations: Executed semantics were shared_initial_candidate (single LLM generation reused across both conditions); the result therefore answers whether post‑generation tooling changes deterministic validator pass/fail for identical candidates, not whether independent agentic, tool‑augmented generation would produce different or safer outputs.
Task bank used deterministic synthetic topology templates and a lightweight simulator; external validity to vendor CLIs, production telemetry, or richer runtime heterogeneity is limited.
Only a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was used; results do not generalize across model families, versions, or scales without replication.

The deterministic validator enforces a specified rule set (workflow/dependency patterns such as shutdown_configure_restore, make_before_break); it cannot exhaustively model all platform or hardware idiosyncrasies.

A ceiling effect occurred: observed baseline success (299/299) violated the preregistered power assumption and makes the originally targeted minimally important effect (pre‑registered +0.20 absolute paired difference) unobservable in this execution.
